courses.name: Personal & Professional Development

content.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
content.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
content.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
content.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics

content.description2: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
content.profile: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
content.topics: Propositional and predicate logic; Truth tables and logical laws; Set theory; Boolean algebra and circuits; Quantifiers; Functions and relations; Proof strategies; Mathematical induction; Recursive definitions; Games without chance and winning strategies; Process modelling
content.methods: Truth-table analysis; Direct proof and proof by cases; Proof by contrapositive and contradiction; Proof with quantifiers; Mathematical induction; Formal process and game modelling

courses.contribution: Directly teaches propositional and predicate logic, quantifiers, truth tables and proof, supplying substantive formal reasoning for philosophical argument. Its further discrete mathematics and game modelling are complementary; it does not supply a complete philosophical-logic sequence.
courses.selectedDescription: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.

courses.name: Governance of Sustainability

content.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
content.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
content.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
content.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

courses.contribution: Makes a specific complementary contribution to public ethics through institutions, power, participation, justice and competing sustainability responses. Governance-framework analysis and policy evaluation test how normative choices enter food, water and energy decisions; this is not a specialist environmental-philosophy seminar.

courses.name: Law, Society & Justice

content.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
content.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
content.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
content.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review

courses.contribution: Makes a specific legal and normative complement through justice, legal positivism, rights, race and gender in law and the relation between law and social control. It connects questions of legitimate authority to actual legal argument without being counted as a dedicated philosophy course.
courses.selectedDescription: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.

courses.name: Modern History

content.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
content.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
content.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
content.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development

courses.contribution: Provides a specific historical complement to political philosophy: modernity, nationalism, liberal and socialist ideologies, imperialism and decolonization, examined through historical contextualization and source analysis rather than as a substitute for the history of philosophy.
courses.selectedDescription: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. courses.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy

content.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
content.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
content.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
content.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis

courses.contribution: Directly examines philosophical justifications and critiques of human rights through natural law, natural rights, positivism, universality and dignity. Legal systems and cases test these claims. This mixed legal/philosophical course adds meaningful normative inquiry beyond the six dedicated philosophy courses.
courses.selectedDescription: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.

courses.name: Comparative Constitutional Law

content.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
content.profile: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.
content.topics: Constitutional origins and fundamental features; Federalism and decentralization; Parliaments and lawmaking; Governments and heads of state; Court systems and judicial review; Constitutional rights; EU constitutional order; Administrative-law functions; Public participation; Administrative remedies; Procedural fairness, discretion and legitimate expectations
content.methods: Comparative constitutional analysis; Constitutional and legislative interpretation; Case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to hypothetical facts; Structured comparative legal writing

courses.contribution: Provides a specific institutional complement to political philosophy through constitutional authority, federalism, judicial review, fundamental rights and procedural fairness. Comparative constitutional analysis gives concrete institutional forms to the rights/authority questions; it is not counted as philosophical theory.
courses.selectedDescription: Comparative Constitutional Law compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. courses.name: Foundations of European Union Law

content.description2: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
content.profile: Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.

content.methods: EU legal-source research; Case-law analysis; Comparative interpretation of EU and national law; Application of free-movement principles to factual scenarios; Structured legal problem analysis

courses.contribution: Provides a specific legal complement to political legitimacy beyond the state through EU competences, subsidiarity, proportionality, citizenship and remedies. Legal-source and case analysis tests how public authority is limited and rights implemented; this does not replace philosophical argument about legitimacy.

courses.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy

content.description2: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
content.profile: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
content.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life
content.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development

courses.contribution: Directly studies historical and contemporary philosophical arguments about knowledge, ethics, mind, freedom, identity, time and meaning through close reading, conceptual analysis and argumentative essays. This substantive foundation is narrower than Radboud’s three-course historical sequence.
courses.selectedDescription: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.

courses.name: Ethics

content.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
content.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
content.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
content.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

courses.contribution: Directly studies moral and metaethical theories through close philosophical reading, comparison and independent argument. Kantian, consequentialist, virtue, feminist and contractarian ethics support questions about value, responsibility and practical judgment.
courses.selectedDescription: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

courses.name: Philosophy of Mind

content.description2: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
content.profile: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. Later inquiries address machine consciousness, virtual worlds, dreaming, perception, transformative experience and the value of experience. Essays develop independent philosophical interpretations and arguments.
content.topics: Persons and personal identity; Psychological and narrative theories of identity; Buddhist non-self; Split-brain cases and self-knowledge; Behaviourism; Physicalism and functionalism; Mind-body problem; Content externalism and internalism; AI intelligence and consciousness; Virtual reality; Dreaming and perception; Transformative experience; Value of conscious experience; Animal minds
content.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual analysis; Reconstruction and evaluation of arguments; Comparison of theories of mind; Literature-based philosophical research

courses.contribution: Directly studies minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary theories, including identity, physicalism, functionalism, perception and machine consciousness. Conceptual analysis and literature-based philosophical essays connect the empirical cognition strand to explicit philosophical argument.
courses.selectedDescription: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.

courses.name: Philosophy of Emotion

content.description2: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.
content.profile: Examines what emotions are and how they shape knowledge, decision-making, ethics, social life and politics. Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories are compared with historical, phenomenological and contemporary accounts. Love, fear, grief, moods and political anger provide focused cases, alongside emotions in art and their changing relation to time. Students analyze texts and emotional vignettes and develop an independent philosophical paper or a project combining argument with creative work.
content.topics: Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories of emotion; Ancient Greek and Indian accounts of emotion; Epistemic emotions; Emotion and decision-making; Love; Fear and existential anxiety; Mood and grief; Moral emotions; Gender and emotion; Political love and anger; Racial injustice; Temporality of emotion; Emotion and artistic expression
content.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual and argumentative analysis; Phenomenological description of emotional experience; Critical comparison of emotion theories

courses.contribution: Directly studies philosophical theories of emotion and their epistemic, moral, social and political significance. Historical and contemporary texts, phenomenological description and independent argument connect feeling, reason, moral judgment and human experience.
courses.selectedDescription: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.

courses.name: Free Will, Time & the Self

content.description2: Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.
content.profile: Explores free will and agency in relation to time and the self. Historical Greek and Indian perspectives introduce debates about fatalism, determinism, compatibility and moral responsibility; later topics include scientific challenges, addiction, luck and agency in games. The second part examines the reality and experience of time, physics and temporal asymmetries, then developing research linking time, action and selfhood. Essays require close source analysis and an independent argument.
content.topics: Free will and fatalism; Foreknowledge and determinism; Compatibilism and rival theories; Moral responsibility; Greek and Indian accounts of agency; Scientific perspectives on free will; Addiction and the self; Moral luck; Games and agency; Value capture; Reality and experience of time; Time and physics; Temporal asymmetries and bias; Time, action and selfhood
content.methods: Conceptual analysis; Close philosophical reading; Argument reconstruction and evaluation; Literature-based philosophical research

courses.contribution: Directly studies free will, agency, determinism, responsibility, time and selfhood through close philosophical sources and independent argument. Scientific challenges and temporal asymmetries are considered within a philosophical investigation rather than counted as a full philosophy-of-science sequence.
courses.selectedDescription: Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.

courses.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy

content.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
content.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.

content.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction

courses.name: Theory of International Relations

content.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
content.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.

content.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting

courses.name: European Union Politics

content.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
content.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.

courses.name: Peace & Conflict

content.description2: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
content.profile: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.

courses.contribution: Makes a specific interdisciplinary complement to public ethics through structural violence, humanitarian law, human rights, reconciliation and transitional justice. courses.name: Introduction to Sociology

content.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
content.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.

content.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

courses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology

Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.

courses.name: Neurobiology

courses.name: Psycholinguistics

content.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

courses.contribution: Provides a specific empirical complement to language and thought through speech production/comprehension, semantics, acquisition, impairments and experimental language research. The full description supports these topics and methods; the course is not relabelled as conceptual philosophy of language.

courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication

content.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.

An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
